abstract: Abstract Introduction Urine samples could partially reflect the renal condition and could provide possible mechanism of high-risk factor for the long-term development of chronic kidney disease (CKD) caused by prematurity. Methods Urine samples were collected from preterm infants (gestational age <28 weeks) when their corrected gestational weeks reached ≥37 weeks. In addition, urine samples were collected from full-term infants beyond 3 days after birth as the control group. The urine proteome was investigated by using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry analysis, and subsequent bioinformatics analysis was performed. Differentially expressed proteins were validated using ELISA. Results A total of 2,634 proteins were identified, 366 proteins were highly expressed in the preterm group, while 102 proteins were enriched in the full-term group. Based on functional analysis, proteins enriched in preterm group were implicated in structure organization, cell adhesion, and extracellular part, while proteins enriched in urine of the full-term group were implicated in the immune response. Kidney inherent cells accelerated into urine have been examined in preterm infants group. Each of the top 20 differentially expressed proteins enriched in the urine of preterm infants was used as a keyword for literature retrieval, ultimately leading to the selection and validation of CDH6 and CDH11 through ELISA. Both proteins were found to be more abundant in the urine of preterm infants than in that of full-term infants. Conclusion The present study provides differences in urine protein profiles between preterm and full-term infants and a new potential explanation for the high risk of CKD development caused by preterm birth.

Methods
This study was approved by the Tianjin Central Hospital of Gynecology and Obstetrics Institutional Review Board (No. 2020KY049). All study protocols adhered to the Declaration of Helsinki, and written informed consent was obtained from all parents of the participants before their inclusion in this study.
Patient Group
The gestational age of all preterm infants was less than 28 weeks, and urine samples were collected from these infants when their corrected gestational age exceeded 37 weeks after birth (kidneys have completed nephrogenesis). In full-term infants, infants with known kidney diseases (acute kidney injury [AKI], congenital nephrotic syndrome, congenital kidney, and urinary tract malformations) and neonatal sepsis were excluded; in addition, infants with urine samples with positive urine protein, occult blood, or white blood cell results were excluded. After exclusion, urine samples were collected on postnatal days beyond 3 to mitigate the influence of maternal factors and delivery-related stress. Finally, five preterm infants and five full-term infants were included in present study.
Urine Sample Collection
Sterile collection bags were utilized for urine collection from each individual infant, with a volume of 2 mL deemed sufficient for subsequent processing. Following the application of collection bags, infants were monitored at 30-min intervals. Upon successful urine collection, samples were promptly transferred to sterile centrifuge tubes and subsequently transported to the laboratory for further analysis.
Urine Sample Preparation
Urine samples from newborns were transported to the laboratory and then centrifuged at 4,000 rpm for 15 min to eliminate cell debris. After that, the supernatants were divided into several aliquots and stored at −80°C until further processing. After thawing, the samples were lysed using SDT buffer (4% SDS, 100 m
m
DTT, 100 m
m
Tris-HCl pH 8.0). Subsequently, the samples were subjected to boiling for a duration of 5 min followed by ultrasonication and another round of boiling for an additional 5 min. The removal of debris was achieved through centrifugation. The resulting supernatant was collected and protein concentrations were determined using a BCA Protein Assay Kit (Bio-Rad, USA). To minimize contamination and protein degradation during urine sample processing, a standardized sterile collection protocol was followed. Urine samples were immediately transported on ice, centrifuged, aliquoted, and stored at −80°C without delay. Although protease inhibitors were not used, low-temperature storage and rapid processing were employed to reduce enzymatic degradation. Nevertheless, we acknowledge that the lack of protease inhibitors may have introduced some degree of protein degradation, which could potentially influence the proteomic results.
Protein Digestion
The filter-aided sample preparation method was used in the protein digestion process [
20
]. The detergents DTT and IAA in UA buffer were used to reduce and alkylate protein solutions. The specific steps are as follows: add an appropriate amount of 1
m
DTT to each sample to a final concentration of 100 m
m
. Incubate in a boiling water bath for 5 min, and then cool to room temperature. Add 200 µL of UA buffer (8
m
Urea, 150 m
m
Tris-HCl, pH 8.0), mix well, transfer to a 10KD ultrafiltration centrifuge tube, and centrifuge at 12,000
g
for 15 min. Add 200 µL of UA buffer and centrifuge at 12,000
g
for 15 min. Discard the filtrate. Add 100 µL of IAA (50 m
m
IAA in UA), oscillate at 600 rpm for 1 min, incubate in the dark at room temperature for 30 min, and then centrifuge at 12,000
g
for 10 min. Add 100 µL of UA buffer and centrifuge at 12,000
g
for 10 min. Repeat this step twice. Add 100 µL of NH4HCO3 buffer and centrifuge at 14,000
g
for 10 min. Repeat this step twice. Add 40 µL of Trypsin buffer (6 µg Trypsin in 40 µL NH4HCO3 buffer), oscillate at 600 rpm for 1 min, and incubate at 37°C for 16–18 h. Replace with a new collection tube, centrifuge at 12,000
g
for 10 min, collect the filtrate, add an appropriate amount of 0.1% TFA solution. Desalt the enzymatically digested peptides using a C18 Cartridge and lyophilize in vacuo. After the enzymatically digested peptides are dried, redissolve them in 0.1% TFA, measure the peptide concentration, and prepare for liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis.
Liquid Chromatography-Tandem Mass Spectrometry Analysis
The Q Exactive plus mass spectrometer coupled with Easy 12 nLC (Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used for the LC-MS/MS process. First, the peptide was loaded onto a trap column in buffer A (0.1% formic acid in water). Second, we used an EASY-nLC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and a self-packed column to perform reverse-phase high-performance liquid chromatography separation at a flow rate of 300 nL/min. Phase A of the reverse-phase high-performance liquid chromatography mobile phase was 0.1% formic acid in water, and B was 0.1% formic acid in 95% acetonitrile. A linear gradient of buffer B was used to elute peptides over 120 min. A data-dependent top 20 method was used to acquire MS data, dynamically choosing the most abundant precursor ions from the survey scan (300–1,800 m/z) for HCD fragmentation. A lock mass of 445.120025 Da was used as an internal standard for mass calibration.
Data Processing
MaxQuant Software (v1.6.0.16) was used to analyze MS data. First, the UniProtKB
Homo sapiens
database was used to search MS data. Selecting trypsin is a digestion enzyme. For database searching, the maximal two missed cleavage sites and the mass tolerance of 4.5 ppm for precursor ions and 20 ppm for fragment ions were defined. Carbamidomethylation of cysteines was defined as a fixed modification, while acetylation of the protein N-terminus and oxidation of methionine were set as variable modifications for database searching. The obtained result was filtered and exported with a <1% false discovery rate (FDR) at the protein- and peptide-spectrum-matched levels. As described previously, label-free quantification was carried out in MaxQuant using intensity determination and normalization algorithms as previously described [
21
–
23
]. In different samples, the “LFQ intensity” of the protein was calculated as the best estimate to satisfy all pairwise peptide comparisons. MaxQuant software was used to weigh and normalize the quantitative protein ratios by the median ratio.
Bioinformatics Analysis
Bioinformatics analysis was conducted in R software (v3.6.3) and packages. When a protein was expressed in at least one sample in the preterm or full-term birth group but not in another group, the expression of this protein in that group was considered specific. Proteins with a fold change ≥1.5-fold and a
p
value <0.05 were considered significantly differentially expressed. The Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed with the “ggplot2” (v3.3.3) and “ggrepel” (v0.9.1) packages. Gene ontology (GO) and KEGG enrichment analyses were carried out with the “clusterProfiler” package (v3.14.3), and Fisher’s exact test and FDR correction for multiple testing were performed. Enriched GO and KEGG pathways were nominally statistically significant at the
p
< 0.05 level. In clinical characteristics of infants, gestational age at birth, birth weight, sample collection time, and maternal age were compared by application the independent samples
t
test (GraphPad Prism, version 5). A
p
value less than or equal to 0.05 was considered significant.
Validation of Differentially Expressed Proteins
In the validation process, urine samples were collected from 18 preterm infants (gestational age <28 weeks) and 16 full-term infants into sterile urine bags. In preterm infants, urine samples were collected when their corrected gestational age exceeded 37 weeks post-birth. For full-term infants, urine samples were collected on postnatal days beyond day 3 to minimize the influence of maternal factors and delivery-related stress. Following collection, urine samples were centrifuged at 4,000 rpm for 15 min at 4°C, and the supernatants were transferred into new tubes and immediately stored at −80°C for subsequent detection. CDH6 (RAB1356, Sigma-Aldrich) and CDH11 (RAB1028, Sigma-Aldrich) were quantified using ELISA kits according to the manufacturer's instructions. Briefly, samples were incubated with HRP-labeled antibodies, followed by the addition of TMB substrate and incubation. Finally, the reaction was terminated, and absorbance was measured using an ELISA microplate reader. Urine creatinine levels were measured using an automated biochemical analyzer (Mindray BS-480) with the use of urine supernatant. The concentrations of CDH6 and CDH11 were normalized to creatinine levels and expressed as CDH6/creatinine and CDH11/creatinine, respectively. CDH6/creatinine and CDH11/creatinine are expressed as means ± SEM.
T
test was used to compare differences between preterm and full-term groups. Differences were considered statistically significant at
p
< 0.05.

Introduction
Based on the development of perinatology and neonatology, the survival rate of neonates, especially preterm infants, has gradually increased in recent years [
1
–
3
]. However, an increasing number of studies have already proven that preterm birth is a high-risk factor for the development of future diseases in various systems [
4
–
10
]. In the field of renal disease, current studies have already proven that preterm birth is a risk factor for long-term chronic kidney disease (CKD) [
6
–
8
]. For example, Crump et al. [
7
] identified that preterm birth had a twofold higher risk of development of CKD than full-term birth in a population-based national cohort.
Currently, the most widely accepted mechanism by which preterm birth could increase the risk of development of long-term CKD is the “nephron number hypothesis,” suggesting that preterm infants have fewer nephrons, thereby increasing their future CKD risk [
6
,
11
,
12
]. However, the detailed molecular mechanism involved in this process has not been clearly clarified.
In full-term infants, nephrogenesis is completed at approximately the 36th gestational week [
11
,
13
,
14
]. In most preterm infants, their gestational age at birth ranges from 21 to 36 weeks, which indicates preterm infant birth with immature kidneys [
1
–
3
,
15
]. Consequently, preterm infants’ kidney should not only need to continue developing, but also must begin performing essential functions such as waste filtration, acid-base balance [
1
–
3
,
15
]. Meanwhile, in full-term infants, the maternal placenta provides assistance to filtration and other roles of kidney. Moreover, preterm infants are often exposed to various stressors including hyperoxia, infection, and pharmacological agents [
1
–
3
]. These two factors likely determine the ultimate trajectory of kidney development. Thus, the major difference between the preterm and full-term kidney is that the preterm kidney undergoes extrauterine development and a stress stage. This abnormal developmental phase affects both the kidney and urine protein profiles.
Since obtaining kidney samples from preterm and full-term infants is challenging, urine samples could be an alternative selection to investigate the distinctive characteristics of abnormal postnatal kidney development in preterm infants. Urine is a crucial sample that partially reflects the kidney condition [
16
]. All kinds of inherent kidney cells or fragments can be detected in urine samples, providing partial insights into the renal status [
16
–
19
]. Therefore, in present study, the collection of postnatal urine samples was conducted in preterm infants at the time when their corrected gestational age reached full term, and in full-term infants whose age matched the previous group. With regard to these extrauterine development and a stress stage, preterm infants born before 28 gestational weeks were selected in present study because they have all undergone similar clinical procedures, such as mechanical ventilation, feeding, infection management, and oxygen therapy [
1
–
3
]. Then, urine samples were collected from preterm infants with gestational age less than 28 weeks and proteomic sequencing was conducted to identify the similarities and differences between preterm and full-term infants. The study design flowchart is presented in
Figure 1
.
Fig. 1.
Flowchart of the study design.
Preterm infants born with immature kidney. During the remaining development stages, preterm kidneys should work independently while developing. At the same time, kidney work was assisted by the placenta while developing. When nephrogenesis finished (corrected gestational age and>36 weeks), urine samples were collected from preterm infants and age-matched full-term infants. Urine proteomics was performed to identify the differences in urine protein profiles between preterm and full-term infants.

Results
Clinical Characteristics of Preterm and Full-Term Infants
Urine samples from 10 newborns (5 preterm infants and 5 full-term infants) were collected at the Neonatology Department of Tianjin Central Hospital of Gynecology and Obstetrics. The clinical characteristics and demographics of preterm and full-term infants are listed in
Table 1
. In brief, the characteristics with statistically significant differences between preterm and full-term infants were gestational age at birth (mean ± SD: 26.37 ± 0.80 vs. 38.28 ± 0.39,
p
< 0.05), birth weight (mean ± SD: 981 ± 154 vs. 3,236 ± 166,
p
< 0.05). There was no difference between these two groups in the sample collection time (mean ± SD: 38.46 ± 0.47 vs. 38.80 ± 0.27,
p
= 0.20) or maternal age (mean ± SD: 30.80 ± 2.39 vs. 30.40 ± 2.88,
p
= 0.82). In addition, maternal complications as well as some detailed information about neonatal morbidity are also shown in
Table 1
. Due to the limited number of referring studies investigating maternal health conditions in relation to offspring urinary proteomics [
24
], we selected preterm infants with fewer maternal comorbidities. However, for extremely preterm infants, it is rare for their mothers to have no comorbidities at all. Therefore, we excluded certain kidney-related conditions, such as maternal hypertension, preeclampsia, and maternal obesity. Nevertheless, in the present study, two out of five mothers had gestational diabetes mellitus, and one out of five had polycystic ovarian syndrome.

Identification of Specific Urine Proteins in Preterm and Full-Term Infants
The PCA analysis performed using the proteomic data obtained by mass spectrometry analysis was able to discriminate preterm infants from full-term infants (
Fig. 2
a). A total of 2,634 proteins were identified by MS analysis, and 2,349 overlapped the preterm and full-term groups (
Fig. 2
b). In addition, 176 proteins were exclusive to the preterm group, and 109 proteins were exclusive to the full-term group (
Fig. 2
b). These exclusive proteins in each group could partially reflect the difference between the two groups. Thus, we performed GO analysis. As shown in online supplementary Figure 1 (for all online suppl. material, see
https://doi.org/10.1159/000548692
), preterm-specific proteins were related to the immune response, while full-term-specific proteins were related to antigen processing. In addition, all of these proteins and corresponding genes are listed in online supplementary Table 1.

Identification and Characteristics of Differentially Expressed Proteins in Urine from Preterm and Full-Term Infants
Proteins with a fold change ≥1.5-fold and a
p
value <0.05 were considered significantly differentially expressed when compared between preterm and full-term groups. As shown in online supplementary Figure 2, 366 proteins were differentially highly expressed in the preterm group, while 102 proteins were differentially enriched in the full-term group. In addition, the top 20 highly significant proteins discriminating preterm infants from full-term infants are listed in
Table 2
. Additionally, comparative analysis was carried out on the functions of the proteins detected in the urine of preterm and full-term infants using the GO and KEGG databases (
Fig. 3
). As shown in
Figure 3
, proteins enriched in urine from the preterm group were implicated in structure organization, cell adhesion, and extracellular part, while proteins enriched in urine of the full-term group were implicated in immune response and extracellular part.

Expression Pattern of Differentially Expressed Proteins in Inherent Kidney Cells
The information detected from urine samples can not only indicate various system condition, but also renal system itself. We addressed differentially expressed proteins identified in urine samples in different types of kidney inherent cells (
Fig. 4
). Enriched molecular lists in each kidney inherent cells referred to our previous study (the previous study provides molecular profiles of the kidney, encompassing both mid and late stages of kidney development, which correspond to the majority of gestational ages in preterm infants) [
25
]. Most of the differentially expressed proteins were enriched in urine samples of preterm infants. For example, CDH11 has already been reported as a biomarker of kidney fibrosis [
26
]. Few inherent kidney cell markers were present in urine samples from both preterm and full-term infants except ATPase H+ transporting V1 subunit G3 (ATP6V1G3), which was highly expressed in intercalated cells of the collecting duct [
27
]. In addition, few proteins expressed in inherent kidney cells were highly present in the urine of full-term infants compared with preterm infants.

Different urine proteins between preterm and full-term infants were addressed in different inherent kidney cell types. Validation of CDH6 and CDH11 by Application of ELISA
In this process, we used TOP 20 differentially expressed protein enriched in urine of preterm infants as a keyword for retrieval, screened out the literature related to the kidney, and then understood whether these proteins might be associated with an increased risk of CKD or kidney development. They could be roughly divided into three categories. First, the molecule has not been reported in the kidney field, including THBS4, KRT13, PCDH18, and TMED3. Second, the molecule has been reported in the kidney field but has no strong correlation with the occurrence of CKD (such as proteins have being only discovered through high-throughput sequencing without validation; or only reported in animal studies without being validated in human studies) including CDH15, MGAM, EFEMP2, ATP6AP1, and ITIH2. Third, protein has been reported to be related to kidney injury or development, including podocyte, glomerular, and tubular injury, CKD risk or kidney development. There are 11 such proteins. Among these molecules, several are involved in multiple situation. These molecules may have a greater chance of being involved in kidney development or an increased risk of CKD. Due to 3 of 20 were cadherin: CDH15, CDH11, and CDH6, which indicated cadherin could be suggest a very important role in this process. Finally, we have chosen CDH6 and CDH11 in validation process by application of ELISA. Urine samples were collected from 18 preterm infants (gestational age <28 weeks) and 16 full-term infants. The expression levels of CDH6 and CDH11 were measured using ELISA. Following normalization to creatinine, the CDH6-to-creatinine ratio was found to be 1.7 times higher in preterm infants compared to full-term infants (
Fig. 5
a). Likewise, the CDH11-to-creatinine ratio was approximately 2.0 times higher in preterm infants than in full-term infants (
Fig. 5
b).

Discussion
Preterm birth has already been identified as a high-risk factor for the long-term development of chronic kidney disease (CKD) [
6
–
8
,
28
–
30
]. However, the detailed mechanism underlying this process has not been well clarified. Due to the difficulty of acquiring kidney samples from preterm infants, urine samples could partially reflect the kidney condition. In the present study, urine samples were collected from preterm infants, and urine proteomics was applied. As a result, differences between preterm and full-term infants in urine proteins have been identified. In addition, acceleration of kidney inherent cells secreted into urine has been examined in preterm infants. Additionally, some potential pathways have been suggested in the present study.
Currently, urine proteomics has emerged as a valuable tool for identifying biomarkers in various nonrenal disorders [
31
–
34
]. Limited studies have already employed urine proteomics methods to discern biomarkers associated with neonatal morbidities, including bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), and AKI [
32
–
34
]. For example, Saima Ahmed et al. [
32
] identified several BPD-associated urinary proteins that predicted BPD risk by application of the urine proteome in 42 extremely low gestational age newborns with a mean gestational age of 26 ± 1.2 weeks . Additionally, in Karl G. Sylvester et al.’s study, researchers validated urine biomarkers that would produce molecular classifiers for both the diagnosis and prognosis of infants with NEC by proteomics analysis [
33
]. Unlike Karl G. Sylvester’s study [
33
], which validated their findings using ELISA, our study focused on presenting the differences between preterm and full-term infants’ urine proteins and analyzing the functional pathways indicated by these differentially expressed proteins. In our study, urine samples were collected from preterm infants with a gestational week less than 28 weeks. In addition, the time points of urine collection were selected after nephrogenesis was completed (corrected gestational week of 37 weeks) when early risk factors for kidney injury, such as infection, hypoxia, asphyxia, and drugs, had already affected the kidney [
1
–
3
,
15
]. At this time, features of urine samples in preterm infants could present causal results. As for full-term infants, urine samples were collected beyond 3 days after birth to eliminate the maternal effect as well as delivery stress. When compared with corrected gestational age-matched urine samples from full-term infants, these differences could provide potential clues to develop a mechanism for understanding the high risk of long-term CKD caused by preterm birth.
Podocytes play an important role in kidney development and kidney diseases, and previous studies have shown that the detection of urine podocytes could indicate disease activity and severity [
16
,
35
–
38
]. In our previous studies, we detected urine podocytes by quantification of podocyte-specific podocin by qPCR [
28
,
29
,
38
]. In that method, the volume of urine from newborns should be less than 30 mL. However, it was difficult to collect such a volume of urine in neonates, especially in preterm infants. One of the initial intentions to explore urine proteomics in preterm infants was to explore podocyte-specific molecules. As a result, as shown in
Figure 4
, several proteins enriched in podocytes could be detected, while specific podocyte proteins were not examined. This result may be because few podocytes were originally included in urine as well as podocyte-specific proteins. In all of these proteins, the only specific kidney cell type marker was ATPase H+ transporting V1 subunit G3 (ATP6V1G3), which is specific for CD-IC [
27
]. In a previous study of ours, we confirmed that podocyte loss plays an important role in development preterm-related CKD [
28
–
30
,
39
]. However, urine protein, which reflects overall kidney function, does not have a very strong correlation with podocyte loss. The high level of urine protein in preterm infants may indicate structural immaturity, glomerular injury, or tubular injury and may represent a poor prognosis. The weak correlation between urine protein and podocyte loss suggests that prematurity not only causes podocyte injury but also some non-podocyte injury. As a marker of the collecting duct, the increased loss of ATP6V1G3 in the urine of preterm infants implies an increase in the loss of intercalated cells and the collecting duct and an increased possibility of injury of collection duct. Both accelerated of podocytes and CD-ICs loss in urine suggests a decrease in functional unit of the kidney among preterm infants, which indicated preterm infants have an elevated risk for developing renal diseases later in life.
The top 20 significantly differentially expressed proteins are listed in
Table 2
. When comparing preterm with full-term infants, the top 20 upregulated proteins are listed in
Table 2
with red highlighting. Among these proteins, 3 of 20 were cadherin: CDH15, CDH11, and CDH6. These CDH family members are significantly correlated with cell adhesion and extracellular matrix organization [
40
]. During nephrogenesis, cell adhesion molecules become evident as epithelial structures differentiate from the induced mesenchyme [
26
,
41
–
43
]. Cadherins are believed to play a crucial role in the metanephric mesenchyme when cells aggregate to form the renal vesicle – a polarized epithelial structure that eventually fuses with the ureteric bud to generate a continuous nascent nephron [
26
,
41
–
43
]. According to current research, CDH6 and CDH11 have been confirmed to be expressed in nephron progenitor cells [
26
,
41
–
43
]. The presence of significant amounts of cadherins in urine may indicate the immaturity of the renal system in preterm infants. Furthermore, CDH6 has been shown to be specifically restricted to the proximal tubule epithelium and is widely recognized as one of the key regulators during this developmental process [
42
,
43
]. The excretion of CDH6 into the urine of preterm infants also suggests greater loss of proximal tubule epithelium, indicating that the nephrons of these infants are more vulnerable to injury. Regarding CDH11, according to the study by Schmidt IM et al., urinary levels of CDH11 were significantly associated with increasing severity of interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy in the kidney [
26
]. Therefore, CDH11 has been identified as a promising noninvasive biomarker for tubular injury. Regarding CDH15, the only related study has shown its involvement in systemic lupus erythematosus and associated glomerulonephritis [
44
]. Thus, CDH15 may represent a potential biomarker for kidney-specific conditions in preterm infants while CDH6 and CDH11 may be more closely associated with CKD risk and kidney development in preterm infants based on current studies. We identified these two proteins using ELISA and demonstrated their increased excretion in the urine of preterm infants. In addition, as indicated by GO analysis shown in
Figure 3
a, functional proteins enriched in urine samples of preterm infants were related to structure organization and cell-cell adhesion. Enriched proteins related to adhesion, structure organization, and matrix organization were still highly expressed in the urine of preterm infants, indicating an elevated risk of abnormal structure in this population. In a study conducted by Sutherland et al. [
14
] renal histopathological examination revealed a higher proportion of morphologically abnormal glomeruli and a significantly larger cross-sectional area of the renal corpuscle in preterm kidneys, suggestive of renal hyperfiltration. Additionally, other studies have reported higher levels of microalbumin and total protein corrected for creatinine in the urine of preterm infants compared to full-term infants, which indicated abnormal filtration in preterm infants [
28
,
45
,
46
]. Thus, the presence of these proteins in the urine of preterm infants offers valuable insights into the underlying factors contributing to elevated urinary protein levels in comparison to full-term infants, while also indicating potential abnormalities in renal structure among preterm infants. In addition to CDH6 and CDH11, there are other proteins among the top 20 proteins that may also be associated with CKD risk and kidney development. For example, both MYH9 and CLEC14A are found in podocytes and are critically involved in the progression of CKD [
47
–
50
]. MYH9 is responsible for encoding non-muscle myosin heavy chain IIA, and mutations in this gene lead to autosomal dominant conditions marked by thrombocytopenia and proteinuria, which can vary in severity from mild to nephrotic syndrome [
47
–
49
]. Research indicates that MYH9 expression is particularly high in fully developed kidneys, mainly within podocytes [
49
]. Additionally, when MYH9 is specifically knocked out in podocytes of mice, it results in spontaneous glomerulosclerosis, flattening of foot processes, and the disruption of slit diaphragm structures, ultimately causing proteinuria and kidney failure [
48
]. MYH9 has also been identified as vital for kidney development [
51
]. As for CLEC14A, studies using models of kidney disease have revealed that its absence worsens podocyte damage and increases proteinuria, highlighting its protective function in renal disorders [
50
]. ANPEP has been linked to various kidney diseases, such as diabetic kidney disease and AKI [
52
,
53
]. Furthermore, significant associations have been found between ANPEP and the risk of CKD [
54
]. Evidence suggests that ANPEP may contribute to CKD progression by influencing inflammatory processes that affect glomerular and tubular functions. Consequently, the presence of these proteins in the urine of preterm infants may serve as an indicator of reduced functional kidney units and warrants further validation to determine whether these markers are associated with an increased risk of developing CKD later in life.
As shown in
Figure 3
b, in urine from full-term infants, highly expressed proteins were related to the immune response. These proteins may come from blood or from the kidney itself. Either source can indicate that the activation state of the immune system was higher than that in preterm infants. In addition to being related to the relatively broad categories of “immune response” and “leukocyte activation,” the proteins enriched in the urine of full-term infants are related to “neutrophils” rather than “lymphocytes.” Based on the research results of David Martino et al. [
55
] on the neonatal immune system, when the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratios is higher, the risk of neonatal infection is reduced, which means that when the percentage of neutrophils is higher, the ability to resist infection is stronger. This is consistent with what our research suggests. There are more neutrophil-related proteins in full-term infants, which can indirectly indicate that their immune ability is higher than that of premature infants.
There are several limitations in the present study. Although PCA analysis showed discrimination between the preterm and full-term groups, the sample size is relatively small. Many pathways did not remain significant after FDR correction for multiple comparisons. Therefore, nominal
p
values (rather than adjusted
p
values) are reported in the main text. In addition, although differentially expressed proteins from urine in inherent kidney cells have been mapped, these cell types are inferred from transcriptomic data and have not been directly linked to the origin of urinary proteins. While some urinary proteins do originate from the kidneys, urinary proteomes represent a systemic profile that includes proteins from both renal and non-renal sources. Thus, this pattern could not accurately define the relationship between urinary proteins and those present in native kidney tissues. In addition, it should be noted that many of the differentially expressed proteins identified in this study, especially those annotated as fragments, immunoglobulin variants, or hypothetical/uncharacterized proteins, have unclear or poorly defined biological functions. This reflects an inherent limitation of untargeted proteomic analyses, which often yield a large number of candidate proteins beyond those that are well characterized. Therefore, the functional relevance of these proteins remains to be validated through targeted experiments and follow-up studies. In this study, we have focused our interpretation on a subset of proteins with known functions and plausible links to kidney development or pathology.
Based on our findings and limitations, future studies should involve larger and more diverse cohorts, stratified by gestational age to enable subgroup analyses of preterm infants (e.g., <28 weeks, 28–32 weeks, >32 weeks) and at different time points (e.g., immediately after birth, weekly intervals, and when corrected gestational age exceeds full term). Additionally, comprehensive data on potential confounding factors – such as maternal health status and neonatal morbidities – should be collected, and advanced statistical methods should be employed to adjust for their influence. Multi-center recruitment will be pursued to enhance cohort diversity and improve the generalizability of findings, where feasible. Moreover, the biological interpretation and validation of the findings should be deepened. In vitro and in vivo studies are planned to explore the underlying mechanisms through which the identified proteins may contribute to CKD in preterm infants. Their potential clinical relevance will also be evaluated, including their utility as CKD biomarkers and as targets for therapeutic interventions. Collectively, these efforts will enhance our understanding of the role of urine proteomics in predicting and managing long-term renal outcomes in preterm infants.
In conclusion, this study provides differences in urine protein profiles between preterm and full-term infants. Additionally, it highlights the potential mechanisms underlying the heightened risk of CKD development following preterm birth, including accelerated excretion of nephron components into urine and increased vulnerability of renal structures observed in preterm infants.
